messages.subject: matrices, vectorization, and parallelism
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Thought I'd revisit this topic. Apologies if it's already been
discussed and I missed it. Looking through (for example)
src/stan/agrad/rev/matrix/multiply.hpp, it seems that we're not
actually calling Eigen to do our matrix multiplies and such. This
obviously precludes our leveraging whatever multicore, SSE, etc.
optimizations that Eigen's got baked in.

My question is: is this an inherent limitation of the current agrad
architecture (which is focused on scalars)? If so, should we consider
revamping the architecture to handle matrices? How much of a colossal
pain would this be? I only ask because the potential payoffs* seem so
large.

Matt

* Potential payoffs that come to mind:
1. We could piggyback on the work that Eigen's done (and will do) to
optimize the hell out of these very important operations.
2. It's fundamentally faster (especially when vectorized instructions
like SSE are available) to work with dense arrays of double values
than with arrays that alternate between packed values and adjoints.
E.g., if we're doing a dot product between two long vectors x and y
the three outputs are dot(x, y), dot(x, y.adj), and dot(x.adj, y). As
it is, all of those dot products has to skip over half of the entries
in each of those arrays, since x[i] is stored right next to x.adj[i].
Those operations should be faster (maybe much faster) if x and y are
stored in separate arrays from x.adj and y.adj.

I agree that there is no shortage of potential payoffs, and I've always thought that we should be using Eigen as much as possible. My latest thought along the lines you describe would be for Stan to extend the Eigen::Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> class so that a Stan::Matrix<double,N,K> instance would either include a pointer to a separate Eigen::Matrix<double,N,K> instance that contained the corresponding adjoints or just included a Eigen::Matrix<double,N,K> of adjoints as a member of the Stan::Matrix subclass. But Bob and Marcus would be the ones who would know how much of a pain that would be to integrate into Stan.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: matrices, vectorization, and parallelism
messages.body_plain:
We could take more advantage of Eigen with the current design if we had a way to allocated large blocks of vari's but it would still be suboptimal.

Changing to something where val and adj were matrices instead of scalars would be a pretty huge change to make but not impossible.  I think the best design would be one where a new class (not inherited from Eigen::Matrix) was created which would store a value and adjoint matrix separately.  In a perfect world this would be able to handle arrays with arbitrary numbers of dimensions and a scalar could become a special 1x1 matrix.

If someone was motivated to do this I would recommend they focus on small test cases first because many of the distributions do some complex things to make them more efficient and it would be easy to get bogged down there early on.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
We have talked about this many times before!

The stumbling block for me is figuring out how
we'd do matrix indexing, which should return an
autodiff var.

On 7/8/13 1:03 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Sunday, July 7, 2013 9:08:45 PM UTC-4, Matt Hoffman wrote:
>
>     My question is: is this an inherent limitation of the current agrad
>     architecture (which is focused on scalars)? If so, should we consider
>     revamping the architecture to handle matrices? How much of a colossal
>     pain would this be? I only ask because the potential payoffs* seem so
>     large.

Yes, they're really big for the matrix multiply part of
the program.  It may even be a speedup for derivatives if
we can calculate the partials using matrix ops, too.

> I agree that there is no shortage of potential payoffs, and I've always thought that we should be using Eigen as much as
> possible. My latest thought along the lines you describe would be for Stan to extend the
> Eigen::Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> class so that a Stan::Matrix<double,N,K> instance would either include a pointer
> to a separate Eigen::Matrix<double,N,K> instance that contained the corresponding adjoints or just included a
> Eigen::Matrix<double,N,K> of adjoints as a member of the Stan::Matrix subclass.

This should be pretty easy for forward-mode, but I
still don't see a clear path to doing it with reverse-mode.

Extending Eigen::Matrix would be problematic because
the results of any operation defined for Eigen::Matrix
would be Eigen::Matrix unless we override everything.

Another option would be to generalize var and vari, which
holds the objects as members rather than extending one and
adding another.  It should be pretty easy for fvar.

   template <typename T>
   struct var {
      vari<T>* vi_;
   }

   template <typename T>
   struct vari {
      const T val_;
      T adj_;
   }

Instead of directly using vari, chainable is what's used
on auto-diff stack for reverse mode, so there's some flexibility.

> But Bob and Marcus would be the ones who
> would know how much of a pain that would be to integrate into Stan.

What I can't sort out is how to do indexing.  We need to
support the following two methods for indexing, and similarly
for other slices like rows and columns.

   var& operator()(int,int);
   var& operator()(int);

where the returned references do the right thing.

We could maybe define a specialized new var as a view.
But then we have to figure out how to allow that to
support all the usual operations, so I can write something
like:

    exp(sigma[1])

where sigma is a vector.  The value for sigma[1] can be
some kind of placeholder, but then we need to define exp()
for that type or somehow figure out how to generalize the definitions.

And once we've done all this, unless we specialize all the
expression templates, we're still back to inefficient compound
operations.

I think the way forward would be to just get it working as a demo
outside of the context of Stan.

- Bob

that the Eigen doc discusses for return types and argument type concepts.

pointed to NONMEM.  In adding ODE solvers to Stan, we want
to be able to do a lot of what NONMEM does but in a much
more general model setting.

   ï¿½ pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) analysis. The software was developed by the NONMEMï¿½ Project

   has relied on the use of the NONMEMï¿½ statistical software for over 30 years.

no-BS sell sheet (Andrew, please browse for both its style
and its relation to our ODE project):

We could recruit a marketing student and produce
something like this for Stan!  Not that I want to sell it
for money, just sell what it can do to potential users and
funders.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob, hopefully you figured it out, but if not, it's just ./model help

For now, I'm assuming the compiled model is located at: ./model

Here are some changes that I want:

1) No arguments stops execution, prints help.
   Current behavior of "./model": runs the model, assumes no data, samples using NUTS2

   Proposed behavior of "./model" is equivalent to "./model help". Does not sample.

2) Get rid of "method=<>". Just make it "<>". The set of things that could fit there (currently) would be: {sample, optimize, test}
   Current command to sample: "./model method=sample" (uses defaults)
   Current command to optimize: "./model method=optimize" (uses defaults)

   Proposed command to sample: "./model sample"
   Proposed command to optimize: "./model optimize"

3) Only allow one of {sample, optimize, test}. Setting two or more should result in no execution, error message.
    Current command: "./model method=optimize method=sample" -- runs the sampler

   Proposed command: "./model optimize sample" -- stops with message like "Only one command {optimize, sample, test} can be called"

4) Restructure help message.
    Current command: "./model help" -- outputs:
Usage: model <arg1> <subarg1_1> ... <subarg1_m> ... <arg_n> <subarg_n_1> ... <subarg_n_m>

Valid arguments to Stan:

  id=<>             Chain id
  data=<>           Input data file
  init=<>           Initialization method
  test_gradient     Check model gradient against finite differences
  random            Random number configuration
  output            File output options
  method=<>         Analysis method

See 'model' <arg1> [ help | help-all ] for argument specific information
 or 'model' help-all for all argument information
Failed to parse arguments, terminating Stan

    Proposed command: "./model help".
Usage: model <arg1> <subarg1_1> ... <subarg1_m> ... <arg_n> <subarg_n_1> ... <subarg_n_m>

Begin inference by selecting one of the following:
  sample            Bayesian inference using Markov Chain Monte Carlo
  optimize          Point estimation
  test              Check model
  help              Prints help

Additional arguments:
  data=<>           Input data file
  init=<>           Initialization method / file
  output            File output options
  id=<>             Chain id
  random            Random number configuration

See 'model' <arg1> [ help | help-all ] for argument specific information
 or 'model' help-all for all argument information

  - Ideally we would replace 'model' with the actually command line call, unless you think that's too messy.

5) Break out "test_gradient" option to "test"/"test gradient"
   Current command to test gradients: "./model test_gradient"
   Proposed command to test gradients: "./model test" or "./model test gradient"
     - "gradient" would be the sub-command to test
     - I'm thinking about future uses where we may build out other types of tests.

6) Fix help printouts. (I killed a lot of the verbose output, but I didn't do it right.) I think the verbosity should be contextually. From the top level, it should just show the simple help, but when called after some options, it should be verbose.

   Current command: "./model method=sample test-all"
      output: "sample"  (this is my fault -- it used to print out information about Sampling Algorithm and get into HMC and NUTS. There wasn't much, but there was a description).

   Proposed command:
      "./model help" prints as above

      "./model sample help" prints the options that can be passed to sample directly.
      "./model sample help-all" prints help novels for each of the algorithms.

7) For the "./model method=sample algorithm=hmc engine=nuts" replace that with "./model sample nuts"
   I guess for sampling, I imagine there being a handful of options: {hmc, nuts, metropolis} and we'll add a few more like rmhmc, rmnuts. I think the settings should be flat after that. I'm not sure it helps to have multiple levels of options configurable in this tool. We would always have complete flexibility in C++.
   The same goes for optimize.
   I think the "sample" and "optimize" commands are just defaults. If someone doesn't play with the parameters, it should always work with just "sample."

Thoughts?

> 1) No arguments stops execution, prints help.
>    Current behavior of "./model": runs the model, assumes no data, samples using NUTS2
>
>    Proposed behavior of "./model" is equivalent to "./model help". Does not sample.

This is new behavior and a break from 1.3.  Personally, I'd prefer to have a default method.

> 2) Get rid of "method=<>". Just make it "<>". The set of things that could fit there (currently) would be: {sample, optimize, test}
>    Current command to sample: "./model method=sample" (uses defaults)
>    Current command to optimize: "./model method=optimize" (uses defaults)
>
>    Proposed command to sample: "./model sample"
>    Proposed command to optimize: "./model optimize"

I can see some of the motivation to removing method, but it does create a singular argument that has to implemented differently from all of the rest.

> 3) Only allow one of {sample, optimize, test}. Setting two or more should result in no execution, error message.
>     Current command: "./model method=optimize method=sample" -- runs the sampler
>
>    Proposed command: "./model optimize sample" -- stops with message like "Only one command {optimize, sample, test} can be called"

Not the desired behavior.  I'm looking into it.

> 5) Break out "test_gradient" option to "test"/"test gradient"
>    Current command to test gradients: "./model test_gradient"
>    Proposed command to test gradients: "./model test" or "./model test gradient"
>      - "gradient" would be the sub-command to test
>      - I'm thinking about future uses where we may build out other types of tests.

My opinion is to go with a categorical argument, test=test_name

We can make gradient the only test here and leave the rest to be added later.

> 6) Fix help printouts. (I killed a lot of the verbose output, but I didn't do it right.) I think the verbosity should be contextually. From the top level, it should just show the simple help, but when called after some options, it should be verbose.

Well, it used to do that.  I'm not sure what changes you've made.

> 7) For the "./model method=sample algorithm=hmc engine=nuts" replace that with "./model sample nuts"
>    I guess for sampling, I imagine there being a handful of options: {hmc, nuts, metropolis} and we'll add a few more like rmhmc, rmnuts. I think the settings should be flat after that. I'm not sure it helps to have multiple levels of options configurable in this tool. We would always have complete flexibility in C++.
>    The same goes for optimize.

I strongly disagree.  Not only do I dislike flattening the sampling options (Riemannian is a property of the metric, not the particular HMC algorithm) but then you have dangling parameters (RMHMC requires fixed point iteration parameters, and if we flatten everything then we have allow other algorithms to have those parameters set or do really awkward parameter validation after the fact.

>    I think the "sample" and "optimize" commands are just defaults. If someone doesn't play with the parameters, it should always work with just "sample."

That is how it currently works, provided we elevate "method" to a special argument that doesn't need the prefix.

> ./models/basic_distributions/normal method=optimize

There's a bug somewhere in the translation of the optimization code.  I thought I had fixed it.

trying to run more than one test at once.

>> 6) Fix help printouts. (I killed a lot of the verbose output, but I didn't do it right.) I think the verbosity should be contextually. From the top level, it should just show the simple help, but when called after some options, it should be verbose.
>>
>>     Current command: "./model method=sample test-all"
>>        output: "sample"  (this is my fault -- it used to print out information about Sampling Algorithm and get into HMC and NUTS. There wasn't much, but there was a description).
>>
>>     Proposed command:
>>        "./model help" prints as above
>>
>>        "./model sample help" prints the options that can be passed to sample directly.
>>        "./model sample help-all" prints help novels for each of the algorithms.
>
> Well, it used to do that.  I'm not sure what changes you've made.

Agreed. that it should be contextual.

>> 7) For the "./model method=sample algorithm=hmc engine=nuts" replace that with "./model sample nuts"
>>     I guess for sampling, I imagine there being a handful of options: {hmc, nuts, metropolis} and we'll add a few more like rmhmc, rmnuts. I think the settings should be flat after that. I'm not sure it helps to have multiple levels of options configurable in this tool. We would always have complete flexibility in C++.
>>     The same goes for optimize.
>
> I strongly disagree.  Not only do I dislike flattening the sampling options (Riemannian is a property of the metric, not the particular HMC algorithm) but then you have dangling parameters (RMHMC requires fixed point iteration parameters, and if we flatten everything then we have allow other algorithms to have those parameters set or do really awkward parameter validation after the fact.

I agree with Michael's disagreement :-)

I only like flattening the top one, ./model sample.
All of the samplers have a similar flavor in terms of their
input and output.  The metric and algorithm (?) make sense
as configurable options.  That's what's so cool about the
way Michael set up mcmc!

>>     I think the "sample" and "optimize" commands are just defaults. If someone doesn't play with the parameters, it should always work with just "sample."
>
> That is how it currently works, provided we elevate "method" to a special argument that doesn't need the prefix.

Agreed.

>> make models/basic_distributions/normal
>> ./models/basic_distributions/normal method=optimize
>

Is the BFGS code not in?  I saw the note on Nesterov.

messages.body_plain:
I do not know what convention to follow in R and I am fine with it.

In RStan, currently if we use function stan_model to create a stanmodel object, there are two methods defined: sampling and optimizing.  For example,

sm <- stan_model(file = 'schools.stan')

fit <- sampling(sm, data = , iter = ,....)

op <- optimizing(sm, data = , method = ...)

So it is like Stan 2.0 though we have a shortcut function stan() that wraps the above stan_model and sampling.  But function stan() cannot do optimization and currently there is no shortcut function.  And now, test gradient is done through sampling function (so function stan can do test gradient) by using argument test_gradient = TRUE.  I can define another function for stanmodel object so we can do

tt <- test(sm, data = ...)

--
Jiqiang

> I have a question about how to extend our base model classes (used
> to do the auto-diff calcs) to allow the log prob function to
> be computed w/o the Jacobian adjustment.
>
> Because we don't want to have to compile different models for
> optimization and sampling, I've modified the code generator so that
> there's a new boolean template parameter, jacobian, in the underlying log probability
> function that is generated from a model:
>
>     template <bool propto, bool jacobian, typename T>
>     T log_prob_poly(vector<T>& params_r,
>                     vector<int>& params_i,
>                     std::ostream* msg_stream = 0);
>
> The parameter jacobian controls whether or not the log Jacobian
> of the constraint inverse transform is added to the log probabilty or not.
>
> There shouldn't be any runtime overhead because it's a static if on
> the template parameter.
>
> The abstract base class for the models (it has the auto-diff code)
> relies on the log_prob function over var, which I've defined to
> include the Jacobian.
>
>     var log_prob(vector<var>& params_r,
>                  vector<int>& params_i,
>                  std::ostream* pstream = 0) {

>                              vector<int>& params_i,
>                              std::ostream* pstream = 0) {
>       return log_prob_poly<true,false,var>(params_r,params_i__,pstream);
>     }
>
> Should we add that to the model along with the matching
> auto-diff versions for gradients?

>
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] out-of-sample predictions
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Jul 13, 2013 at 11:07 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Use the generated quantities block.  You can have random
> functions of parameters and data and it's only computed
> once per saved sample.
>
> There's as of yet no good way to prevent the duplication
> of the likelihood part of the model to generate new data.
>
> For cross-validation, though, you need to have something
> higher level to divide up the data into folds, but
> each model itself can do predictive inference using
> the generated quantities block.
>
> For a logistic regression hard coded with a quadratic of
> a single predictor, you'd do this:
>
> data {
>   ... as before ...
>   int<lower=0> N_twiddle;       // # of points to predict
>   vector[N_twiddle] x_twiddle;  // data for which to make predictions
> }
> parameters {
>   ... as before ...
> }
> model {
>   ... as before ...
> }
> generated quantities {
>   vector[N_twiddle] y_hat_twiddle;  // predictions
>   for (n in 1:N_twiddle)
>     y_hat_twiddle[n] <- inv_logit(beta0 + beta1 * x_twiddle[n] + beta2 * beta2 * x_twiddle);
> }
>
> This saves the probabilities in y_hat_twiddle, but you might want
> to do sampling, depending on the application, in which case you could
> do:
>
>    y_hat_twiddle[n] <- bernoulli_rng(inv_logit(...as above...));
>
> where bernoulli_rng generates a binary value which is 1 with the
> specified probability.

Two questions:

- We had once talked about being to do

 y_hat_twiddle[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(...as above...));

to do that in the generated quantities block.  Is that the case?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] [stan-users] out-of-sample predictions
messages.body_plain:
It's one of our research goals to program an operation like rep[y] that will do posterior predictive replications.  This is related to our "network of models" idea.

On Jul 13, 2013, at 12:27 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:

>
>
>
> On Sat, Jul 13, 2013 at 11:07 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > Use the generated quantities block.  You can have random
> > functions of parameters and data and it's only computed
> > once per saved sample.
> >
> > There's as of yet no good way to prevent the duplication
> > of the likelihood part of the model to generate new data.
> >
> > For cross-validation, though, you need to have something
> > higher level to divide up the data into folds, but
> > each model itself can do predictive inference using
> > the generated quantities block.
> >
> > For a logistic regression hard coded with a quadratic of
> > a single predictor, you'd do this:
> >
> > data {
> >   ... as before ...
> >   int<lower=0> N_twiddle;       // # of points to predict
> >   vector[N_twiddle] x_twiddle;  // data for which to make predictions
> > }
> > parameters {
> >   ... as before ...
> > }
> > model {
> >   ... as before ...
> > }
> > generated quantities {
> >   vector[N_twiddle] y_hat_twiddle;  // predictions
> >   for (n in 1:N_twiddle)
> >     y_hat_twiddle[n] <- inv_logit(beta0 + beta1 * x_twiddle[n] + beta2 * beta2 * x_twiddle);
> > }
> >
> > This saves the probabilities in y_hat_twiddle, but you might want
> > to do sampling, depending on the application, in which case you could
> > do:
> >
> >    y_hat_twiddle[n] <- bernoulli_rng(inv_logit(...as above...));
> >
> > where bernoulli_rng generates a binary value which is 1 with the
> > specified probability.
>
> Two questions:
>
> - We had once talked about being to do
>
>  y_hat_twiddle[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(...as above...));
>
> to do that in the generated quantities block.  Is that the case?
>
> - Is this actually in 1.3?  I seem to recall it being in develop but not released yet.  If not we really need to get a release out soon.  Are we only blocking on the arg refactor or is there something else we're hoping to land before 2.0?
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>

messages.subject_clean: designs: generated model concept + template code org
messages.body_plain:
I'm driving toward the model concept (in the C++ sense)
described here:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Model-Concept

The main differences from what we have now are:

   1.  no more virtual functions, no more log_prob_grad
       intermediate base class;  I'll probably get rid
       of the log_prob base class.  All classes and functions
       using models now have a template parameter for the
       model class.

   2.  templated methods for log prob with
       a template param to suppress the Jacobian adjust
       for transformed params (suggestions for the param name
       would be appreciated --- it's now jacobian_adjust_transforms).

   3.  only a minimal set of functions remain, with other
       functionality pulled out into statics that take the model
       class as a template parameter and the model as an argument.

There's no overall loss in functionality.

One advantage of pulling out the utilities into statics
is that conceptually at least, the generated model class
without the main only depends on std::vector and stan::math
(and any probability function used).

If we can organize the necessary template code for
VectorView and OperandsAndPartials, we should also be able
to have a probability lib that doesn't depend on our
var or fvar.

I organized the new functor-based definition framework that way:

    branch:   feature/functor

Function definitions don't depend on var or fvar, and you only
pull in the metaprogramming libs for those types if you need them.
It's pretty easy to do this with argument-dependent lookup.

I'd like to get VectorView and OperandsAndPartials into the
same shape (and also renamed out of camel case!).
The specializations of these classes to var and fvar then
go in stan::agrad namespace and in their own files.  The
result is a cleanly separated math lib and var and fvar
lib.

Even if nobody uses just the double-only versions, it seems
like a reasonable way to me to organize the code to minimize
dependencies.    For instance, HMC doesn't need to bring in
fvar, so incompleteness in the fvar lib won't restrict usage
of HMC as it would if we just continue to pile in functions.

- Bob

Sorry -- the "short description" was something that wasn't well thought through. We can drop that. Comments:
- the model displayed in the help should be displayed for the "Usage: model..." line also.
- the model name is incorrect. I think we should be grabbing the command line call, not the model name. I compiled 'models/basic_distributions/normal' and I'm seeing the help line as 'normal_model'

Daniel

messages.subject: the Bugs models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I was just thinking . . . we have various people implementing the Arm models, which is fine, but for marketing Stan, I'd really like to have the graph showing Stan's performance compared to Bugs/Jags on the Bugs/Jags models.  For this, we should do the best we can.  This means using Jags's starting points (where available), also using things like vectorization that will make Stan faster.  This helps for speed, also will help users if they are using these as templates.  I'm not saying we need to knock ourselves out optimizing every model, I'm just saying that if someone goes though and does a good job with the basics (vectorization, the use of compound forms such as bernoulli-inv-logit or whatever it's called, and the use of the Matt trick where appropriate), this should help.
I think it would be worth a lot to us to have a slam-bang graph showing our performance vs Bugs/Jags on their home turf.
A

messages.subject: Re: the Bugs models
messages.body_plain:
I agree that we should optimize the BUGS examples (perhaps in addition to literal translations). But I don't think the corpus of BUGS models makes for a very good benchmark. The models are a lot simpler than the substantive stuff that we see on the list and generally have small amounts of data.

I don't think they were ever intended to be used for benchmarking as much as to demonstrate features of the BUGS language (mostly to biostat researchers). And we should be emphasizing to a more general audience features of the Stan language, which I think are better, unless you are a person who has spent a lot of time absorbing the BUGS language and doesn't want to spend even a little bit of time learning how Stan differs.

Anyway, we already have (somewhat outdated) walltimes on the BUGS (plus a few other) models at

https://code.google.com/p/stan/wiki/SpeedResults

and for the vast majority of them, the execution time is just negligible, even if it may be a lot faster or slower in relative terms than what some flavor of BUGS does. But they are dwarfed by the compilation times, so you have to get into whether the compiled model is going to be called multiple times in addition to the effective sample size thing (I think Mike has some benchmarks on that). For the more complicated models that we see on the user list, the compilation times can be negligible relative to the execution times.

For a speed or effective sample size per time benchmark, I think it would just be better to draw data from some populations that are generated by common GLMs. And have graphs showing how the objective trends as the number of observations and / or the number of predictors increases.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: the Bugs models
messages.body_plain:
I just don't know what point there is to make with the BUGS examples that couldn't be made better with constructed data. You here a lot of people say that BUGS is too slow, but I've never heard any one say that the BUGS examples are too slow. So, these people must be talking about a situation that is qualitatively different than what is covered by the BUGS examples. And we think we know pretty well what causes BUGS to be slow: Either many parameters that can't be block-updated (walltime) or highly correlated parameters (effective sample size). And we know that Stan is less susceptible to those things. So, let's just show that with a few graphs.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: the Bugs models
messages.body_plain:
I don't think it is a killer pitch to say that for some BUGS example that Stan can get 2000 effective samples per second while BUGS can only get 1800. Computational statisticians look at that and would say that Stan is 11% more efficient. But for someone who thinks a BUGS example is a remotely relevant benchmark, that will likely reinforce their belief that they should just stick with BUGS. To them, one second of execution time is plenty to make inferences either way, but Stan has a 25 second penalty for compilation time and requires them to spend a day learning a somewhat different syntax.

Doing a BUGS benchmark certainly doesn't preclude us from doing relevant benchmarks, but it may undermine the message of the relevant benchmarks.

Ben

On Tuesday, July 16, 2013 1:37:06 PM UTC-4, Peter Li wrote:
> Should we organize the models by chapter and include R code for whatever
> figures/graphs are provided in the book--this is how the online BUGS/R
> code for the book is organized?

I think we created some confusion where several of us are working on stuff that is loosely related to the Applied Regression Modeling book.

This repo that just got created

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstanarm

is where I am implementing an R package that depends on (R)Stan but does not require the user to write a .stan model in order to use.

Rather we take an existing function like glm() and

1. Make a similarly named function like stanglm() that
2. Takes all the same arguments as glm() in the same order and
3. Adds additional arguments to the end that pertain to the prior so that
4. It can be called like

fit <- stanglm(RTEN ~ INTG + ORAL + WRIT, data = USJudgeRatings)

and it will estimate the corresponding model (now by MCMC) via Stan instead of what glm() does (which happens to be IRLS). Later we can add an option to do MAP, VB, etc. via Stan.

Rather than have the user write a .stan model, we write a .stan model that sits in the exec/ subdirectory that is both optimized and very abstract so that (approximately) one model can handle all of the options supported by the R function we are emulating. In practice, I had to write a separate gaussian.stan file and a discrete.stan file to cover stanglm() because family = gaussian() implies that there is an extra sigma parameter that is not present when family != gaussian(). The .stan models we write are wrapped up into empty stanfit objects when the rstanarm package is installed.

Anyway, anyone is welcome to contribute to this. In particular, Alexej possibly has been doing something along these lines. But as far as I understand, Peter has been doing something different, namely taking the models in the ARM book and writing .stan implementations. That is fine, but should go into stan/src/models/arm .

Ben

messages.subject: implicitly-defined parameters
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, July 16, 2013 3:36:18 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> n 7/16/13 2:01 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> ...
> > 1. The case where a transformed parameter is an implicit function of data and parameters
> >
> > |
> > parameters {
> >    real alpha;
> > }
> > implicitly defined parameters {
> >    real<lower=l,upper=u> beta;
> >    beta <- implicit( pow(beta, 5) - beta - alpha); # or something
> > }
> > |
>
> I take it this means beta is the solution to:
>
>     beta = beta^5 - beta - alpha.

The solution for beta on (l,u) defined by

beta^5 - beta - alpha == 0

> Can there be whole systems of equations?

I suppose, but I think by far the most common is just one equation.

> Does anyone have an application for this?

In statistics or economics, it is usually some weird exact constraint on the parameters that has to be satisfied. These are a little easier to deal with if you are using ML because you only need the constraint to bind at the optimum and can use penalization and stuff to enforce it.

Also, some distributions do not have a closed-form PDF but may have a closed-form characteristic function or inverse CDF, such as the generalized lambda

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tukey_lambda_distribution

in which case, given a data point and the parameters, you have to solve for the implicitly-defined quantile, q,

x - icdf(q, parameters) == 0

in order to evaluate the density as a function of q (which is known in closed-form).

> Any idea how we'd implement implicit functions in general?

The are usually not too difficult to solve numerically. Boost has root finders

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_54_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/internals1/roots.html

So, the question is how to is the user to communicate what arbitrary equation is to be solved. I guess we would have to parse something in the .stan file into a callable.

Or maybe this is a candidate for the model.hpp mechanism we talked about before where if model.hpp is in the same directory as model.stan the make call is

$(CC) -include model.hpp -o model $(CFLAGS) model.cpp

so we would just need to explain what model.hpp needs to #include to get it working.

> Sorry if we've discussed it before --- I was very confused about
> what implicit meant in the auto-diff context.

The main thing is Stan needs to know when it is dealing with an implicit function. In the above case where

x - icdf(q, parameters) == 0

you can pretty easily solve for q* on (0,1) such that this equation holds to machine tolerance, but q* is a function of the parameters. So, if you change a parameter slightly, you change q*. Thus, you have to take the derivative of

x - icdf(q, parameters)

with respect to each of the parameters and divide by the (negative of the) derivative with respect to q (at q*) in order and stick that into the autodiff expression tree in order to (correctly) evaluate the derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameters.

So, that is really a pretty different animal than an ODE, aside from the fact that in both cases you can't write what you don't know as an equation in terms of what you do know.

Ben

Thanks!  That's exactly what I needed to understand
what we need to auto-diff.

Yes, very different than ode.  But we might
want to use some of the same syntax for defining
equations

For syntax, since both the ode and implicit equations
define functions, some kind of function-definition syntax
seems appropriate, then you could use the function in
the code.

For the simpler case, just calling a root function might
work:

   root(real beta) in { beta^5 - beta - alpha = 0; }

The icdf case seems one step more complicated in that
the function you care about is itself expressed as a derivative.
It would be nice to be able to do that, too.  In fact, it's
what we need to do for the better approach to ode where we
take a Jacobian of the equation, then integrate the ode and
its Jacobian (and use the Jacobian in the solver).  It's a lot of
auto-diff, but it should be doable.

messages.subject: almost there on model refactor
messages.body_plain:
I'm almost ready to wrap up the generated model refactor
in a pull request.  It's in branch:

    feature/issue-112

I've managed to simplify the code, remove a bunch of files, and factor
the meta programs so that there are no more dependencies on stan::agrad
anywhere in the generated model code.  If we can remove the agrad dependencies
in the probability libs, we should have very clean dependencies (and I
think we can by implementing OperandsAndPartials and VectorView appropriately).

I wrote the following Wiki page to illustrate what the model
currently does.

   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Model-Concept

If nobody objects, I'm going to further trim the generated code
by moving most of the remaining methods to static functions so that
the model itself doesn't know about writing to CSV format, but rather just
how to extract parameter names and dimensions into std::vector objects.

Comments appreciated, or if you don't care, I should have this
finished up by the end of the week.

This will also fix the issue with not checking dimensions properly

messages.subject: model refactor & doc
messages.body_plain:
The model refactor is up to date with the main develop
branch now, and unless someone has more suggestions, I'll
go ahead and create a pull request.

This is on branch:

     feature/issue-112

Issue 112 is removing Jacobian adjustment for optimization.
There's now a template parameter.  It also fixes Issue 151,
testing matching sizes for vector assignment.

I've updated the Wiki, which describes both the generated model
code concept and the external utility functions that do some of the work
that used to be done by member functions:

     https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Model-Concept

I also radically trimmed down the code generated by the model
and separated out some of the metaprograms into math and agrad
components.  The latter was for cleaner organization, but the upshot
is that the current model concept does not import anything from agrad
(though the utility functions do).

I also tried to rename things to be a little more coherent,
but I'm not totally happy with the results.

- Bob

P.S.  I have no idea how we did anything before being more disciplined
       with branches.  This one should probably be rebased before the merge.

messages.body_plain:
I just pushed a bunch of updates - aside from testing and doc this should be considered a first "draft".  Let me know if you prefer any tweaks to the output.

Regarding testing, the only question is just how much we want to test.  It's straightforward to take a configuration from samples.csv, turn it into an argument string, execute a test model, and then compare the consistency of the original configuration and the Stan output.  But how many configurations should we test?  Would it be enough to just test one configuration for each method, i.e. sample, optimize, and test?  If we wanted more, should we test every combination or just enough combinations so that every argument is used at least once?

On Mon, Jul 15, 2013 at 4:21 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
>
> On 7/15/13 10:22 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> ...
>
> >     - I'm still in favor of dropping the "method=" for the analysis methods. I see the point about the implementation
> >     having to treat it differently, but if we could, I'm in favor of dropping it.
> >
> >
> > That has been fixed -- I think you missed an intermediate email.
>
> Great!
>
>
> >     - I'm seeing this as front end code and making it simple for a user. If a user wanted to do RMHMC, I wouldn't expect
> >     comprehension of the structure of our command line arguments for the parent options in order to get how to use
> >     RMHMC. With regards to design for the algorithm, of course this is a good thing. I'm just thinking about using Stan.
>
> Well, they may not comprehend it, but if it's there, it
> makes it easier on the development side.   How it's documented
> and understood by users is a different issue.
>
> For git, what you have is:
>
>    git <git-options> command <command-options>
>
> Things like logins are in git-options and anything command-specific
> in the command options.
>
> Git's own help, which you run as:
>
>   > git help <command>
>
> does not document the git-options, just the help-specific ones.
> Basically each <command> gets a man page.
>
> Other than naming the command options coherently across commands,
> I don't see that there's much we can do.  We can doc families of
> commands that have similar options together.
>
>
> >     Also, it makes it easier writing coherent doc if every analysis method is treated as its own. I know, this means for
> >     duplicated doc, but there shouldn't be too many options, right? We're not talking hundreds.
>
> We just had a similar discussion on the list about propagating
> the ~ syntax to each and every distribution's doc.  So far, no
> feedback from anyone on that, so I'll probably do it.
>
> Having said that, the big issue with cut-and-paste is that it
> makes any modifications going forward much harder.
>
> All things being equal, simplicity for the user is a good
> tiebreaker.  So definitely the help options for a subcommand
> should dump everything out
>
> - Bob

Yes, but if you have 10 methods with 5 binary parameters, that's 10 * 2^5
rather than 1 method with 10 parameters, which is 2^10.

But what if the parameters are continuous?  We have to use some judgment to
test reasonable values, like negative ones if there's a positivity constraint.

>     My main concern is the pure number of tests, but if that's not a concern let me play around a bit.  I'm pretty sure

> interface also doesn't take much time.

Yup -- those aren't the bottleneck.  It's all the compilation.

> We'll need to test enough of the options one way or another. Embedded options makes sense to a certain degree, but I
> think the tests should be the same no matter how we implement it under the hood.

Yes, but we can also make the tests more modular if the code's
more modular.  We can't just test everything.  For the code
where there's different behavior at different scales (like log1m(x),
which goes to second-order Taylor series then first-order), we test
where we know scales change.

- Bob

messages.subject: clarifying error messages (again!)
messages.body_plain:
Dan Stowell's recent post highlighted just how opaque our
error messages can be in context:

   Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis
   rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue
   (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Error in
   function stan::prob::normal_log(m): Location parameter (max size) is
   256, but must be consistent, 1 or max=768
   If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a
   problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
   If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be
   drawn from the posterior.

   Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial
   values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the
   model.

I had to grep for the message in our code and then reason backwards.

What's happening is that the model is throwing an exception at every log
probability evaluation when given inconsistly shaped and sized inputs.
Therefore the initializer can't find a valid place to start.

We should find some language to clean up both of these messages
in our next release and put them in the doc.  For the first message,
we might want to add to the other suggestions:

   check that all functions and distributions have consistently sized,
   in-support arguments

and for the second message

   a function was called with arguments of different scalar, array, vector,
   or matrix types, and they were not consistently sized;  all arguments
   must be scalars or multidimensional values of the same shape;  found dimensions=
   <list of argument shapes passed in>

I'll add it to the to-do list for 2.0 on the Wiki.

- Bob

messages.subject: No std::cerr/std::cout; EXPECT_EQ vs. EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ
messages.body_plain:

two guidelines:.

     EXPECT_EQ to compare discrete values.

     There's no way to get it back to R and so on.

     The ONLY place it should show up is in the
     top-level commands that write to the command line.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Handling errors in our agrad libraries
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Handling errors in our agrad libraries
messages.body_plain:
On the one hand, throwing errors is the best thing to do
to diagnose problems in a Stan model.

On the other hand, not throwing errors is consistent with
the cmath lib, which is probably what a C++ client using our
auto-diff would expect.

Now can we throw our errors, but somehow doc how to config
things globally to have the lib behavior?

That should make everybody happy.

The big problem with throwing exceptions from functions is figuring
out where they came from.  So a lib function calling sqrt()
should check the input before calling sqrt() so it can throw a more
informative error.

- Bob

messages.subject: eigen Ref and MatrixBase
messages.body_plain:
There's this discussion:

   http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicFunctionTakingEigenTypes.html

and then the doc for Ref:

   http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/classEigen_1_1Ref.html

which seems to get around the hack in the functions doc.

To make good use of either of these, it would seem to me that
we'd need our functions called in Stan to return Eigen expression
templates.

We can do this by grabbing the traits for the matrix, which
will give us the underlying Scalar type as well as
RowsAtCompileTime and ColsAtCompileTime (1 or Dynamic).

I'm not sure how helpful it would be without having mixed
type expression templates.

For example, a simple regression coeff-matrix product beta * X,
you want to avoid copying an intermediate for beta * X, but
beta is going to be a var and X a double, so we can't use
Eigen's built-in product expression template as we'd like to in:

    y ~ normal(beta * X, sigma);

- Bob

On Monday, July 29, 2013 1:34:42 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I remember you wanted this, but I still don't even
> understand what is a non-square Cholesky factor is.

If L is MxN with M > N, then

Sigma = L * L'

is a MxM covariance matrix that happens to be singular (actually that is true regardless of the constraints on L). Ostensibly, you could take the LDL' factorization of that Sigma (Eigen actually does pivoting for numerical stability so it would be PLDL'P' where P is a permutation matrix). If you construct the matrix

L * sqrt(D)

then you get a MxM lower-triangular matrix whose last M - N columns are all zero. You could then drop the zero columns to get a MxN Cholesky factor.

> QUESTION FOR EVERYBODY:
>
> 1.  Do we need non-square Cholesky factors?  (I'm assuming
> the answer is yes to this, though I don't know why.)

Yes, they are used in factor models (and some other economics stuff) where you have the functional form

Sigma = Lambda * Lambda' + Theta

where Lambda is lower-triangular with positive diagonal elements but not necessarily square and Theta is diagonal with positive diagonal elements. Then, you can write the likelihood of a sample covariance matrix given Sigma.

> 2.  Which syntax:
>
>      a.  two data types
>
>          cholesky_factor[K]
>          rectangular_cholesky_factor[M,N]
>
>      b.  one data type
>
>          cholesky_factor[M,N]
>
>      c.  one data type overloaded for dimensions
>
>          cholesky_factor[K]
>          cholesky_factor[M,N]
>
> b. is the easiest to doc assuming the answer to 1. is yes.

I think c is best but b is okay, particularly if the parser could say something like "you put cholesky_factor[K], maybe you meant cholesky_factor[K,K]?"

> I couldn't find anything in the Wikipedia under Cholesky
> factorization or triangular matrices.
>
> What are the constraints?  Specifically, if the Cholesky factor
> is M x N, what are:
>
>    * constraints on M and N

I think M >= N is okay. I have never seen the M < N case actually used, and it would be weird because there would be more free elements in L than in Sigma.

>    * elements constrained to be zero

All cells where the column index is greater than the row index.

>    * elements constrained to be positive

All cells where the column index is equal to the row index.

> For square ones, my understanding is that M == N, L[m,n] == 0 if n > m,
> and L[m,m] > 0.
>
>  From the example, I gather M >= N, L[m,n] == 0 if n > m, and L[m,m] > 0.
> Is that right?

Yes.

On 7/29/13 2:47 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, July 29, 2013 2:41:16 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>     A lot of code gets touched by the declared data types and I
>     haven't added one in ages, so needed to refresh myself on
>     the layout anyway.
>
>
> In which case, we probably need a wiki page on adding data types.

:-)  It'll have to get in line behind the other doc projects
in the works (like the Stan paper, RStan paper and auto-diff doc,
all of which I'd rather do first).  None of the relevant code is
documented conceptually, so this would require
documenting the readers, writers and transforms as a basis.

It's probably a higher priority to document how to write a distribution,
too.  That's a lot more complicated with the vectorization.

You can find the places where code needs to go by grepping for
cov_matrix.

First I have to finish testing the square case.  Then I'll try
to get the non-square case working.

> Another thing that we need is the Cholesky factor such that
>
> |
> L * L'
> |
>
> is a correlation matrix. Attached is a R function that does so in the square case so that it doesn't get lost.

We'll need to work out the Jacobian.

And the non-square case if you want that.

We'll also need a name for the correlation matrix case when I get
around to coding it.  Should we anticipate this type and adopt
a suitable naming convention to begin with for the cov case?

   cholesky_factor_rectangular_cov[M,N]
   cholesky_factor_cov[M]

   cholesky_factor_rectangular_corr[M,N]
   cholesky_factor_corr[M]

I'm still not sure about overloading the syntax for square and
rectangular versions --- I'm worried it'll be confusing.

This might all have to wait until after 2.0 --- it's turning
into a huger project than the couple of days I anticipated.

I was hoping to also get to the lp__ replacement, but maybe that
and correlation matrices Cholesky factors can wait until after 2.0.

I was also hoping to get forward-mode auto-diff done for 2.0,
but that's probably also going to have to wait.

- Bob

messages.subject: double and leading underscores (from Eigen list)
messages.subject_clean: double and leading underscores (from Eigen list)
messages.body_plain:
See the message from Eigen below the sig.

I had no idea about this convention, but it looks like we
should:

   * rename all variables that begin with underscores

   * rename all variables with double underscores

The first is an internal implementation detail that's pretty
easy to fix.

The second is a big fix requiring messing with the generated
code.  It also forces the lp__ fix.

Should we aim for 2.0?

I could turn my attention from the Cholesky factor (which is
independent and can wait to be generalized) to this.

C++ sure is messy (edited for publication from what I
really think).

- Bob

MESSAGE FROM EIGEN:

On Tue, Jul 30, 2013 at 8:10 AM, Hauke Heibel <hauke....@gmail.com> wrote:

> I want to suggest that we refrain from using leading underscores in the
> future because of clause 17.4.3.1.2/1 which states that ...
>
> Certain sets of names and function signatures are always reserved to the
> implementation:
>
> * Each name that contains a double underscore (_ _) or begins with an
> underscore followed by an upper-case letter (2.11) is reserved to the
> implementation for any use.
> * Each name that begins with an underscore is reserved to the implementation
> for use as a name in the global namespace.
>
> In particular the first bullet point can lead to issues and did so on Cygwin
> which did not like the variable name _X. My suggestion to completely stop
> using leading underscores is just a precaution in order to prevent any
> future issues.

I agree, we've been too easy on that. A simple:

grep -e "[ (,_]_[a-zA-Z0-9]" Eigen/* -R

tells me there are numerous such occurences!

gael

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] double and leading underscores (from Eigen list)
messages.body_plain:
I would file this under the "nice to work towards and cleanup as we can, but not critical" heading and put it off until after 2.0 because:

1) we've not seen any problems due to our use of this,
2) it sounds like Eigen hasn't seen any big problems either, they're just being pedantic and precautionary, and
3) variable names with leading/trailing underscores is a widely used convention so, regardless of what any standard says, it's unlikely that a compiler will all the sudden completely choke on this.

That said, given the version number bump, getting rid of lp__ would be nice to do before 2.0.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Personally I'd be in favor of the function-like call.  That way we're not intruding any new features to the language.

On Jul 31, 2013, at 7:47 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I have a question about syntax for the increment log prob
> and also just want to make sure the following plan is OK with
> everyone, as it will have a big impact on our syntax going
> forward.
>
> Right now, I have a new feature branch that provides a statement
>
>   increment_log_prob(x);
>
> where x is any expression.  I added a deprecation warning for direct use of
> lp__, but plan to leave lp__ in place for the 2.0 release.   So this model:
>
>
>  parameters {
>    real y1;
>    real y2;
>    real y3;
>  }
>  model {
>    y1 ~ normal(0,10);
>
>    increment_log_prob  normal_log(y2,0,1);
>
>    lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log(y3,0,1);
>  }
>
> generates this warning (not an error, so it doesn't stop parsing):
>
>
>  WARNING:
>    Direct use of variable lp__ is deprecated and will be removed in a future release.
>    Please use increment_log_prob(u) in place of of lp__ <- lp__ + u.
>
>
> but compiles, with all three lines producing the same effect for
> their respective variables.
>
> QUESTION 1:
>
> Is this parens-free syntax with one token with underscores OK?
>
> I could add a colon:
>
>   increment_log_prob:  normal_log(y2,0,1);
>
> and also remove spaces:
>
>   increment log prob:  normal_log(y2,0,1);
>
> or write it out more like a function (my original inclination but
> it seemed cluttered):
>
>   increment_log_prob(normal_log(y2,0,1));
>
> Or we could suggest writing it this way:
>
>   increment log prob:
>     normal_log(y2,0,1);
>
> or really anything.
>
>
> QUESTION 2:
>
> Should I vectorize it?  That is, what can the argument be?  Right now,
> it's a single real value.   I'm inclined to keep it that way because
> we don't have any functions that return matrices, vectors, or arrays of
> probabilities.
>
> So the syntax would be:
>
>  for (n in 1:N)
>    increment_log_prob
>      normal_log(y[n],0,1);
>
> rather than:
>
>  vector[N] buffer;
>  for (n in 1:N)
>    buffer[n] <- normal_log(y[n],0,1);
>  increment_log_prob
>    buffer;
>
>
> NOTE (relevant to QUESTION 2):
>
> Right now the code being generated is simple, but I'm about to implement
> Marcus's suggestion of accumulating the log probs in a buffer and then
> using sum() to dump them out in an efficient expression template for auto-diff.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] increment_log_prob vs. lp__ design questions
messages.body_plain:
It's a new feature in that it's a new kind of statement
no matter what the syntax is.  There aren't any other functional
statements like this anywhere.  Unlike C++, Stan doesn't let you
just use an expression as a statement (like a void-return function).

But I'm OK either way.  Given that I'm on the fence between using
parens and not, I'm happy to go with parens if you have a strong
opinion and nobody else cares.

Anybody else want to weigh in?  (This is easy to change before
2.0.)

- Bob
